Baby & Child

When do baby teeth fall out?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Baby teeth usually begin to loosen around age six, but the change to adult teeth takes several years. Knowing the broad sequence can help you support your child without turning the chart into a deadline.

Two sets of teeth, with a few years of overlap

A first loose tooth can feel like a major milestone. Baby teeth, also called primary teeth, help a child chew and speak and preserve space while the jaws and permanent teeth develop. They need care even though they will eventually be replaced.

There are usually twenty primary teeth. They commonly start appearing around six months and are generally all present by about age three. Shedding often begins around six and continues into the early teenage years, with several years when baby and permanent teeth share the mouth.

Most children have twenty-eight permanent teeth by the early teens, excluding wisdom teeth. Thirty-two is the total only when all four third molars develop and are included; it is not a number every thirteen-year-old should already have.

Why a baby tooth becomes loose

As a permanent successor develops and moves toward eruption, the baby tooth’s roots are gradually resorbed. Less root remains to anchor it, and the crown eventually loosens within the surrounding gum. This explains why a naturally shed tooth may look as though it has little or no root.

Eruption is the name for a tooth emerging into the mouth; shedding means a primary tooth coming out. The two events are related but do not have to happen on the same day. A gap can remain while the permanent tooth continues to move into place.

Children may be excited, cautious or upset about the change. Explain what is happening without promising that it must follow exactly the same timetable as a sibling or classmate.

Typical timing for upper baby teeth

The following ranges describe when primary teeth usually appear and are lost. They are a guide, not a deadline for each child.

Upper central incisors: appear at 8–12 months; shed at 6–7 years.

Upper lateral incisors: appear at 9–13 months; shed at 7–8 years.

Upper first molars: appear at 13–19 months; shed at 9–11 years.

Upper canines: appear at 16–22 months; shed at 10–12 years.

Upper second molars: appear at 25–33 months; shed at 10–12 years.

Typical timing for lower baby teeth

Lower central incisors: appear at 6–10 months; shed at 6–7 years.

Lower lateral incisors: appear at 10–16 months; shed at 7–8 years.

Lower first molars: appear at 14–18 months; shed at 9–11 years.

Lower canines: appear at 17–23 months; shed at 9–12 years.

Lower second molars: appear at 23–31 months; shed at 10–12 years.

Use these ranges with the dentist’s assessment of the whole mouth. Overlap between ranges means there is not one compulsory order for every tooth.

The front teeth usually lead the change

The lower central incisors are often the first baby teeth to appear and the first to loosen, around six or seven. The upper central incisors commonly follow. Lateral incisors, the teeth beside the central pair, are often lost around seven or eight.

This broadly resembles the early eruption sequence, but it should not be treated as an exact replay. Upper and lower teeth do not always follow the same order in every child.

A little tenderness can occur around a very loose tooth. Significant pain, swelling or a child avoiding food deserves dental advice rather than being dismissed as an inevitable part of growing adult teeth.

Baby molars are replaced by premolars

Primary first molars commonly shed around nine to eleven, while the canines and second primary molars are often lost between about nine and twelve. Their timing overlaps, so a canine may be lost before or after a neighbouring baby molar.

The permanent teeth that replace baby molars are called premolars. Permanent molars are additional teeth that emerge farther back as the jaw grows; they do not take the place of baby molars.

The first permanent molars often arrive around six or seven, behind the last baby teeth, without any tooth falling out first. Second permanent molars tend to arrive around eleven to thirteen, with upper and lower ranges differing slightly. Watch for these new back teeth when helping with brushing.

Let a wobbly tooth progress naturally

The AAPD Foundation advises allowing a loose baby tooth to fall out on its own. A child may gently move it with the tongue, but there is no need for a parent to force, twist or attach string to it.

If the tooth is painful, remains troublesome or seems to block a permanent tooth, let the dentist examine it. A retained primary tooth sometimes needs professional help, but that decision should follow an assessment.

Keeping the child involved can reduce worry. Explain that they can tell you if eating or brushing hurts, and avoid making removal into a test of bravery.

Care after a tooth comes out

A small amount of bleeding may follow natural shedding. With an adult supervising, a clean folded piece of gauze can be held with gentle, steady pressure at the area. Remove the gauze after bleeding settles; do not leave loose gauze in a child’s mouth during sleep.

Avoid poking the gap or repeatedly rinsing and spitting while it is bleeding. A cool damp cloth can offer comfort. Strong or persistent pain, swelling or bleeding that does not settle with pressure warrants advice from a dentist.

A salt-water rinse is not a required immediate step after every naturally lost tooth. After a dental extraction, follow the dentist’s specific instructions; postoperative advice commonly avoids vigorous rinsing on the day of the procedure. Only use a rinse when the child can reliably spit it out and the dental team recommends it.

An injury is different from normal shedding

A baby tooth lost early through decay or an accident may leave space that neighbouring teeth can move into. The dentist may consider a space maintainer, depending on the tooth, age and development of the permanent replacement. It is not needed for every naturally lost tooth.

If a tooth is knocked out, seek urgent dental advice. Never put a baby tooth back into its socket, because this can harm the permanent tooth developing beneath it.

A knocked-out permanent tooth is a time-sensitive emergency. Handle it by the crown, not the root. If you cannot safely replace it or are unsure which type it is, keep it in milk and contact an emergency dentist immediately. Do not leave it dry while trying to identify it.

Wisdom teeth usually come much later

Third molars, commonly called wisdom teeth, usually appear in the late teens or early adulthood, if they erupt at all. A commonly used development chart gives seventeen to twenty-one as a typical range, but timing varies.

Some people develop fewer than four wisdom teeth or none. Others have teeth that remain within the jaw or only partly emerge. Their familiar name reflects the later age at which they arrive; it does not measure intelligence or maturity.

Not all wisdom teeth need removal. The dentist considers position, disease, symptoms and whether the area can be kept clean. Teeth that remain in place still need monitoring.

When your child’s timetable looks different

Early and late patterns both occur. A child whose first teeth arrived later may also shed them later, but this is not a guarantee about each tooth. A missed birthday target alone cannot diagnose a dental problem.

Discuss concerns at regular visits rather than waiting a fixed extra year. Earlier advice is sensible when the two sides develop very differently, a permanent tooth appears behind a baby tooth that is not loosening, a tooth was lost early, or a gap seems unusually prolonged.

Pain, swelling, injury or signs of infection should not wait for a timetable comparison. A dentist can decide whether observation or an X-ray is appropriate; images are not automatically needed for every variation.

Protect the teeth that are staying and the teeth still to come

Arrange the first dental visit when the first tooth appears and no later than the first birthday. Six-monthly check-ups are common, but the dentist should set the interval according to the child’s needs and risk of decay.

Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste. For children under three, use a rice-grain-sized smear; from three to six, use a pea-sized amount. Supervise brushing and help clean where teeth touch. Ask the dentist about the appropriate routine as the child becomes more independent.

Limit frequent sugary snacks and drinks, and remember the newly emerging permanent molars at the back. A changing smile still needs consistent care: the aim is comfortable eating and healthy teeth, rather than making every milestone happen on schedule.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Development charts show typical ranges, not exact deadlines.

Permanent molars emerge behind baby teeth; premolars replace the primary molars.

How BeMama can help

Ask your child to show you where the new back teeth are, and help brush those areas while celebrating the changing smile at their pace.

When to seek help

Seek dental advice for significant pain, swelling, persistent bleeding or injury. Never reinsert a knocked-out baby tooth; urgent care may save a permanent tooth.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Twenty baby teeth usually give way during childhood and the early teens.
  • Early teens commonly means twenty-eight permanent teeth, excluding wisdom teeth.
  • The first adult molars may arrive without a tooth falling out.
  • Let a loose tooth come out naturally and keep brushing gently.
  • Routine dental visits matter even when the timetable looks typical.

Frequently asked questions

Which baby tooth usually falls out first?

Often a lower central incisor, around six or seven, although individual order varies.

Do all children lose their first tooth at six?

No. Six is a common starting age rather than a deadline.

Why does the tooth seem to have no root?

Its roots are gradually resorbed as the permanent successor develops, allowing the baby tooth to loosen.

Do adult molars replace baby molars?

No. Premolars replace baby molars. Adult molars erupt farther back in the mouth.

Can an adult tooth appear before any baby tooth falls out?

Yes. First permanent molars often arrive behind the baby teeth around six or seven.

Should I pull out a loose tooth?

Let it fall naturally. If it hurts or causes problems, ask the dentist rather than forcing it.

Should I rinse immediately when a tooth falls out?

Manage any bleeding gently first and avoid vigorous rinsing or spitting. Follow specific aftercare if the tooth was extracted by a dentist.

Should a thirteen-year-old have thirty-two teeth?

Not necessarily. Twenty-eight excludes wisdom teeth, which generally appear later and do not develop in everyone.

Do I have to wait a year before asking about delayed eruption?

No. Raise concerns at a dental visit, and seek earlier advice for pain, swelling, injury or a marked difference between sides.

What if a baby tooth is knocked out in a fall?

Do not put it back. Contact a dentist urgently for injury assessment and advice about the developing adult tooth.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
